Q762.L1t: The passage is a first-person account of a teenager who takes pride in being a good big brother to his younger siblings.
Q762.L2t: The author's brother was hit by a pick-up truck at age nine and has used a wheelchair for six years.
Q762.L3t: The author says he watches over four sisters and a brother besides himself, which makes six children, and a family like this would very probably also include two parents.
Q762.L4t: Counting the author, his four sisters, his brother and probably two parents, the family has eight people.
Q762.L2f: The author's brother was injured in a swimming accident at school and has used a wheelchair for only one year.
Q762.L3f: The family consists only of the siblings the author looks after, and neither the author himself nor any parents are counted as members of it.
Q762.L4f: The family is probably the smallest possible group, made up of just the four sisters and the brother the author looks after.

Q851.L1t: The Spring Festival is China's most important traditional holiday, a time for family reunions and festive customs.
Q851.L2t: Chinese New Year's Day is calculated by the Chinese lunar calendar, and in 2015 it fell on February 19.
Q851.L3t: The celebrations traditionally begin on the 23rd day of the 12th lunar month and end on the 15th day of the first lunar month, and a lunar month lasts about 29 to 30 days.
Q851.L4t: Traditionally the festival lasts about twenty-three days, from the 23rd of the twelfth lunar month to the 15th of the first.
Q851.L2f: Chinese New Year's Day is calculated by the solar Gregorian calendar and falls on the same date every year.
Q851.L3f: The traditional festival is defined by the national holiday, which runs from the Eve to the seventh day of the first lunar month, with no celebrations before or after.
Q851.L4f: Traditionally the festival lasts only about one week, ending when offices and schools reopen after the seventh day of the first lunar month.

Q961.L1t: Tort law decides when a person who injures another through careless or wrongful conduct must pay damages.
Q961.L2t: Violating a safety statute can amount to negligence per se, but courts recognize certain excuses for the violation.
Q961.L3t: An emergency not of the actor's own making excuses a statutory violation if the actor behaves reasonably, and here the car went out of control despite the husband's reasonable efforts while he rushed his child, who had stopped breathing, to the hospital.
Q961.L4t: The driver will not recover, because the husband acted reasonably in a genuine emergency, which excuses his crossing of the center line.
Q961.L2f: Negligence per se arises only when the statute expressly creates a private right to sue for damages.
Q961.L3f: Once the husband's car crossed the line, the oncoming driver had a final opportunity to avoid the collision, and that doctrine bars recovery regardless of the husband's emergency.
Q961.L4f: The driver's claim fails because the driver had a final opportunity to avoid the crash and did not take it.
